na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c0.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Fungi form their own kingdom of life, separate from plants and animals. They cannot make food from sunlight; instead they release enzymes and absorb what they digest outside their bodies.\n\nThey include mushrooms, moulds and yeasts. Scientists have named about 150,000 species, but there may be millions more.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c1.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: The main body of a fungus is the mycelium, a web of microscopic threads called hyphae. It spreads through soil, wood, leaf litter or food, mostly out of sight.\n\nHyphae grow at their tips and can fuse with each other, building networks that explore the ground for food.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c2.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: A mushroom is a fruiting body: the part a fungus builds to spread its spores. It can appear overnight because it swells cells that have already formed with water.\n\nA single mushroom may release billions of microscopic spores, carried away by air, water and animals.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c3.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Wood is hard to digest because of lignin, a tough material that stiffens plant cell walls. Fungi are the main organisms able to break it down completely.\n\nWithout them, dead trees would pile up for centuries, and the carbon and nutrients locked inside would be slow to return to the soil and air.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c4.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Most land plants, around 80–90% of species, live in partnership with fungi in and around their roots, called mycorrhiza. Fungal threads extend the roots' reach far into the soil.\n\nThe plant pays in sugars from photosynthesis. The fungi bring water and nutrients such as phosphorus, and can help plants cope with drought and disease.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c5.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: A lichen looks like one organism but is a partnership: a fungus living with algae or cyanobacteria. The fungus gives shelter; its partner makes food from sunlight.\n\nTogether they grow on bare rock, bark, roofs and tundra, from deserts to Antarctica. Many are sensitive to air pollution.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c6.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Yeasts are single-celled fungi. One species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has worked for humans for thousands of years, raising bread and fermenting beer and wine.\n\nToday it is also one of biology's most important lab organisms, and it is engineered to make medicines such as insulin and vaccines.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c7.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Fungi fight bacteria and each other with chemicals, and some have become life-saving medicines. Penicillin, from a Penicillium mould, launched the age of antibiotics.\n\nOther fungal molecules now prevent the rejection of transplanted organs and lower cholesterol. The search for new drugs in fungi continues.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c8.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: In the Blue Mountains of Oregon, USA, a single honey fungus, Armillaria ostoyae, spreads under the forest over almost 10 square kilometres. It may be several thousand years old.\n\nBy area it is one of the largest living organisms known. Above ground you see only clumps of honey-coloured mushrooms in autumn.

na-fungi.title: na-fungi.c9.text
Fungi: the hidden kingdom: Some wild mushrooms are delicious; others can kill. The death cap, Amanita phalloides, causes most fatal mushroom poisonings, and it grows in Portugal under oaks and other trees.\n\nNo simple test tells safe from poisonous. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified it in person.
